working_title: The Serial Killer Who Was a Cotton Swab
alt_title: Police Hunted a Woman Who Didn't Exist
subject: 'Phantom of Heilbronn': from 1993 to 2009, police in Germany, Austria and France linked the same unknown female DNA profile to roughly 40 crime scenes, including the 2007 killing of police officer Michele Kiesewetter in Heilbronn. In March 2009 investigators concluded the DNA came from contaminated cotton swabs, traced to a worker at the factory that packaged them. The Kiesewetter killing was later attributed to the NSU terror cell (2011).
why_potential: One of the best 'twist' payoffs in true crime: the most wanted woman in Europe was a manufacturing contaminant. Object-led (swab, lab, map of crime scenes), no gore, no private suspect to name (the factory worker is NOT named). Demand for this exact case not measured, but DNA/forensics twists perform in the niche.
hook_15s: 0-2s: A cotton swab under a lab lamp; VO 'Police hunted this woman for 16 years.' 2-6s: Map of Europe fills with 40 red pins. 6-15s: 'Her DNA was at murders, burglaries, car thefts — in three countries. Nobody ever saw her. In 2009 they found out why.'
structure: Pins spread across Germany, Austria, France (1993-2009)
Strange pattern: crimes with nothing in common
2007 Heilbronn police officer killing raises the stakes (memorial card, no detail)
Twist: DNA came from the swabs themselves — factory contamination (worker not named)
Aftermath: Heilbronn case later linked to the NSU; forensic swab standards changed (verify)
Prompt: 'How many other cases did this touch?'

working_title: The Queen of Crime Vanished for 11 Days
subject: On the night of 3 Dec 1926 Agatha Christie left her home in Sunningdale, Berkshire; her car was found next morning at Newlands Corner, Surrey, near the Silent Pool. A huge public search followed. On 14 Dec she was found at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel in Harrogate, registered under the surname of her husband's mistress (Neele). She never publicly explained the episode; amnesia was the official account.
why_potential: Celebrity + genuine unexplained mystery + no victim = fully ad-safe and broadly appealing; the hotel-register name is a perfect single strange detail. Strong comment driver (amnesia vs. revenge plot vs. publicity). Demand not measured by a captured reference.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Abandoned 1920s car on a frosty hill, headlights still on; VO 'The world's greatest mystery writer disappeared.' 2-6s: Newspaper-style search map. 6-15s: 'December 1926. Thousands searched for 11 days. When she was found, she'd signed in under one very strange name.'
structure: Twist: the name in the register

alt_title: The First Fugitive Caught by Wireless
subject: London, 1910: after music-hall singer Cora Crippen ('Belle Elmore') disappeared, Dr Hawley Crippen and Ethel Le Neve fled on the SS Montrose to Canada, Le Neve disguised as a boy. Captain Henry Kendall recognised them and sent a wireless telegram; Inspector Walter Dew of Scotland Yard took a faster ship and arrested them on arrival in Canada. Crippen was convicted and hanged (Nov 1910); Le Neve was acquitted. A 2007 mtDNA study claimed the remains were not Cora's — disputed.
why_potential: A chase where the detective overtakes the fugitive across the Atlantic thanks to new technology; a disguise detail; and a 2007 DNA twist that reopens the case. Ships/ocean/wireless are excellent pipeline fits. Remains in cellar must not be shown or described.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Ship's wireless key sparks in the dark; VO 'This message caught a fugitive in the middle of the ocean.' 2-6s: A 'boy' on deck whose suit doesn't fit. 6-15s: 'Summer 1910. A captain recognised two passengers — and Scotland Yard raced them across the Atlantic on a faster ship.'
structure: Disappearance of Cora Crippen (no detail of remains)
Dew's faster ship overtakes; arrest in Canada

working_title: An Entire Colony Vanished — and Left One Word
subject: Roanoke colony (present-day North Carolina): about 115 English settlers arrived in 1587 under governor John White; his granddaughter Virginia Dare was the first English child born in the Americas. White sailed to England for supplies; war with Spain delayed his return until August 1590, when he found the settlement deserted and 'CROATOAN' carved into a post — without the agreed cross that would signal distress. Their fate is unknown; archaeological work continues.
why_potential: Iconic single-word cold open, no violence, and a 'missing distress signal' clue that viewers love to debate. Highly animatable (palisade, carved post, ocean, coastline map). Mystery rather than murder — slight niche-fit penalty.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Torch light crawls over a carved wooden post: C-R-O-A-T-O-A-N. VO 'Over 100 people vanished. They left one word.' 2-6s: Empty palisade in fog. 6-15s: '1590. Their governor came back three years late. One sign was missing — the one they'd agreed meant danger.'
structure: White leaves for supplies; war delays him
Theories: moved to Croatoan Island / joined inland groups / lost — labelled

working_title: Caught Because of How He Wrote One Phrase
alt_title: The Unabomber's Manifesto Gave Him Away
subject: The 'Unabomber' mailed or placed bombs from 1978 to 1995, killing three people and injuring 23. In 1995 the Washington Post (with the New York Times) published his manifesto; David Kaczynski and his wife recognised the writing style and ideas, and contacted the FBI. Linguistic comparison — including the unusual form 'you can't eat your cake and have it too' — supported the case. Ted Kaczynski was arrested at his Montana cabin in April 1996, pleaded guilty in 1998 and died in 2023.
why_potential: Forensic-linguistics twist (a phrase as evidence) is clever and non-graphic; cabin + typewritten pages animate well. Constraints: domestic-terrorism topic is advertiser-sensitive; victims acknowledged on a card; brother's decision framed respectfully (he is a living public figure via his own advocacy).
hook_15s: 0-2s: Typewriter keys strike '...eat your cake and have it too'; VO 'He was caught by the order of six words.' 2-6s: FBI case map of 17 years. 6-15s: 'For 17 years the FBI couldn't find him. Then newspapers printed his 35,000-word manifesto — and one reader recognised the voice.'
structure: A family member recognises the writing
Linguistics: the phrase and other matches
Arrest at the cabin (1996), guilty plea (1998)
